utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 6th of October, 2009. Let me first greet you, Professor. Good afternoon to the accused, the Defence counsel, Mr. Scott and his case manager, and my greetings to all the people assisting us. I think you have two IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The Praljak Defence has filed their objection to a document submitted by the Prosecution for Witness Zrinko Tokic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1071. And the Prosecution has submitted their objections to Praljak Defence's list of documents tendered through Witness Tokic, Zrinko. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1072. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Very well. We're going to start the examination of the expert witness, cross-examination, that is. We have received a binder. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Scott. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Yesterday, I read out to the witness his curriculum vitae and some documents, and they were supposed to be admitted as IC documents. Unfortunately, at the end of that part I forgot to request for the documents to be marked for identification, so I am kindly asking for the documents to be admitted as IC documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number for identification, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document just mentioned by counsel shall be given Exhibit IC1073. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've already heard it said in the courtroom since yesterday a number of times, as I hope you appreciate by now, our time is limited, and I'll be most grateful if you can please give concise answers to my specific questions, if you'll listen to my question carefully. And if I need you to say something more to expound on it or give it a further explanation, then I'll certainly ask you to do that. But I would greatly appreciate your assistance if you can do that. Just on a preliminary matter and just to make sure that I have a couple of basic details correct, sir, both from your CV and from your testimony yesterday, I have your date of birth as being the 2nd of September, 1954; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I get the name of your father, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any military training or service experience, sir, in connection, presumably, prior to the time that you began your academic work or at some point along the way? Did you have any military service?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I served in the JNA in 1980, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was a period of the compulsory service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the time-period? You say 1980. Was it for the calender year 1980?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it was from the end of 1979 to the end of 1980. I was supposed to serve for a year, and I only served 10 months. The compulsory service lasted for 15 months, but for those who had graduated from a university, it was 12 months. And as I left the JNA, I had a rank of a non-commissioned officer. I was a lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I was just going to ask you a bit more about that. So you told us you left the service, your active service, with the rank of lance corporal. Did you receive any particular training or expertise, any particular specialisation in connection with your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the lowest rank in the JNA after special training. That was all I had. I did not undergo any further military training, and I did not get any other ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. My question was a bit less focused on rank and whether you were, as part of your service, given a particular area of specialisation. For example, did you receive any training in artillery? Did you receive any training as an infantry soldier? Did you receive any training as a communications officer? Any area of specialisation?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I was an infantry lance corporal, which means that I underwent infantry training, but it was a specialist training. Recruits are earmarked in advance to undergo training for lance corporals. I was one of those who underwent such training in the Republic of Slovenia in a place called Vipava.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you serve in the Croatian armed forces at any time during the war? And for these purposes, when I say "during the war," I'm talking about the period 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I found myself in the Ministry of Justice and Administration, in its Department for the Implementation of Penal Sanctions, and I stayed there until September 1992. That was the time of the most fierce conflicts, and I was involved in those. In September, I became the assistant minister of justice, which means that I was the head of the prison system in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm sorry. Let's just take it a piece at a time. You've just told us that -- you said the height of the conflict, or at least at that particular period, if I heard you correctly, was in September 1992, and you said something to the effect of, I was involved in that. You then immediately said that also in September, you were assistant minister of justice, so let me clarify. How or in what role were you involved in the conflict in September 1992 or around that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time. At the time, I wasn't, Counsel. That was the Government of Democratic Unity or the popularly known war government. After the agreement was reached between the minister of justice and the minister of defence, as I was the head of the prison system and the judiciary police, which under the law which prevailed in Croatia at the time was the third military formation, they formed several units, and in the month of March 1992 they formed a brigade, the 98th Brigade, which was a reserve brigade of the Croatian Army composed of judiciary police and other staff members of the prison system. And in order for --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. As I've said, we have to be -- we have to mind our time quite carefully, please, and you've answered my question. Was it in connection within that service that you subsequently were awarded the rank of colonel by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was promoted to the rank of colonel because in the month of March 1992, or, rather, the beginning of 1992, I was appointed as the person who could provide orders to the soldiers of that brigade, and then I was promoted to the commander of the brigade. Since the commander of that brigade could not be a person without rank, I was offered the rank of brigadier, in view of my high education. I said, jokingly, that I wanted to be a colonel, although that was a lower rank, and then they gave me the rank of a colonel in order for me to be able to command that brigade. President Tudjman gave me the rank of a reserve colonel of the Croatian Army. As the assistant minister and the commander of the brigade, I was in charge of the judiciary police which partly participated in the Croatian defence war and partly guarded prisoners in the Croatian prison system. It should be noted here that some of the prisoners at the beginning of the war, when I was still not the head of the prison system, were abolished, and those were prisoners who were charged with less serious crimes. This is something that is customary in every war, that prisoners are amnestied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And apart from continuing to serve in your duties in connection with the Ministry of Justice and the Croatian penal system, were you involved in any military operations, combat operations, if you will, in connection with the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I did not participate in combat operations. I only supervised the training of that brigade and its deployment to certain war zones, operations zones. Those were operations as in Slavonia, in Lika, and on the southern front. Soldiers who were in that brigade were placed under the direct command of those operations zones who were in charge of their deployment and their combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly to say that, then, you were involved in the training of these soldiers, but once they were sent out in the field, into particular operational areas, they were actually placed under the command of someone else?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I did not participate in their training. I supervised their training. And it is true that they were placed under the direct control of other commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for what period of time were you involved in that function, sir? Just give me a year. All I need are just approximately from a date -- from one date to another date?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that was from the 16th of January, 1992, to the end of the month of June 1992. That brigade was then disbanded pursuant to the decree of the Ministry of Defence and the government. All such units were disbanded because the system --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to look in the binder to -- you'll have a binder there in front of you that has numbers on the tabs, and the way we'll proceed is if you can turn, please, to the tab that's marked 3D03727. My apologies, my apologies. Well, let me refer to that. I don't know if we need to turn to it. That's a copy of your CV. I'm not sure that we really need to look at it, but if I can just refer to that, sir. In your CV, you indicate that you were awarded with a certificate of participation in the homeland war. Now, was that certificate of participation in connection to what you've just told us, this six months of some sort of supervisory capacity concerning this brigade? Is that the service for which you received the certificate of participation?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I received the lowest certificate and award, and everybody who were with me in the staff and supervised that brigade received the same certificate. When the brigade was disbanded, we received those certificates, the lowest recognition one could obtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer to my question, sir, it would have been briefer if you could have just said, Yes, the answer to my question was yes. All right? So if you could turn in the binder to P11016, P11016. And on that page, sir, do you see this is a record -- this is part of the "Official Gazette" from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P11016. It's also on the screen in front of you, if that will be faster, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that, sir -- is that the -- on that gazette, we have the English translation, but about the middle top of that page -- the middle column of that page, does that include you as item number -- as one of the number 2s in the first group in connection with your appointment or award of the rank of colonel by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with -- going back to your period, for a moment, to the time when you were -- from 1984 to 1991, you've told us that you were in the Croatian Ministry of Justice as head of the Department for Offenders Treatment, which is also reflected in your CV, and then you've told us that from 1991 to 1992, you were an assistant minister of justice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part about the assistant is correct. However, I was the head of that department from 1986 to 1991. I was the head of the Department for Treatment, and I -- just one department in the judiciary system, and that is one department that supervises all experts in the judiciary/prison system. And after that, I was an adviser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I now discover that you were deputy minister of justice. You could have mentioned that in your CV, which would have helped us save time. As such, as deputy minister for justice, did you meet the deputy minister for defence, General Praljak? At the level of the Croatian government, would deputy ministers meet or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not deputy minister of justice. I was an assistant minister for just one sector. In the Ministry of Justice, there were different sectors in the Ministry of Justice, and I was assistant minister for the implementation of penal sanctions. I did not deputise for the minister; therefore, I did not participate in the government session and I did not have meetings with other ministers and deputy ministers. I only supervised the prison system, and within the context of the brigade I also supervised the deployment of that brigade and its training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you fail to mention this in your CV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my curriculum vitae it says that in 19 -- or, rather, that I worked in the Ministry of Justice, and I believe that it does say that I was an assistant minister. I've never hidden that. It says that in my curriculum. It says that I was commended. I didn't mention the rank of a colonel in my curriculum because this is not scientific information. This is not something you volunteer in your scientific CV. This was part of my patriotic duty. I joined the defence at the moment when Croatia was at a risk and when it faced total Serb aggression, and I did not and I do not believe that this is an important part of my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can refer you to 3D03727, page 3D42-6773, and here you will see, under "Employment," "Assistant minister and activities social science." That is what you will find in the original CV which has been submitted as a document accompanying the expert's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the President's questions, however, and just to round this off, as I look at your CV - and I confirm it again now - you didn't say anything in your CV about your military service or your rank of colonel. You don't think that's material information that someone reviewing your CV would want to know about?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, my CV is a scientific CV. I have been offering it to the scientific world for 30 years, and what I sent to the Trial Chamber is my CV that has been published on the web, that everybody is familiar with. The details that you mention would be listed in a CV that would have other purposes rather than scientific purposes. The Trial Chamber did not request from me to specify those things, and the Defence team didn't do it either. I have never hidden this fact. On the contrary, I'm very glad that I was an active member in the defence of Croatia in those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you had these positions with the Ministry of Justice and you were involved with the penal system or the treatment of offenders, isn't it the case, sir, that you became the subject or have been the subject of some controversy over your involvement in those matters at the time and in connection with your work and the processing of political prisoners and dissidents?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, during the totalitarian regime in Croatia it was not only my dilemma, as I worked in that system, it was the dilemma of everybody in Croatia regarding the processing of political prisoners. I have to say that while I worked in the Ministry of Justice, I did not have any contact with political prisoners and I never worked with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean by you had a dilemma, sir? What dilemma did you have in that regard ?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we spoke about two phenomena tied to information conformity. One is public giving in and the other is privately accepting facts. My dilemma was that I never publicly accepted some things. I never publicly accepted -- or, rather, I never privately accepted the fact, but I publicly conformed, like everybody else in Croatia, when this was in keeping with the job that I did. What I did in the Ministry of Justice was closely tied to what I was interested in, and that was social psychology, and working in that area, I acquired the status of a recognised expert for the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I know you want to talk about that, and you mentioned that yesterday, but let's stay on topic. You said you had a dilemma, and what you're telling us, sir, in so many words is you were in a situation where what you were required to do in connection with your job was directly in conflict with your personal feelings and values; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, while I worked in the justice --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question is rather simple --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- nobody ever asked me to get engaged in such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- excuse me, sir, excuse me. I've asked you now several times, please. Listen to my question and please answer my specific question. If I want to ask for an explanation, I will. If the Judges want to have more information, thy will certainly intervene. The question that I put to you now only calls for a yes or no. You've told us, sir, that you felt you were in a dilemma that you said everyone was in at the time because you had to conform to working in that system. You did things that you had to do for your job, but privately, in your soul, whatever one might want to call it, you felt conflicted; correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I can't answer by just yes or no. I didn't do that. If I'd done that, I don't know whether I would have accepted to do it. If somebody had forced me to do that in the system of justice, I would probably not have accepted the job, but I can't be sure. So my dilemma was not whether to do something that was not in conformity with my humanitarian positions. I was not put in such a position. If I had, I don't think I would have done it even at a risk of some consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling the Judges, under oath, that you have not been the subject of a controversy reported in the Croatian media about your involvement in these matters?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, this has nothing whatsoever to do with what you just asked me a little while ago. I am under oath, and I've been telling the truth. If you're asking me about the media, it's a different thing, it's a different category. Ask me about the media, and then I will answer your questions about the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I -- I would like to ask both of you, as usual, that please kindly slow down. Especially our expert should take this into account, that the interpreters have got some difficulties to follow you when you talk very quickly, and also, of course, as usual, you have to stop -- both of you have to stop between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, unfortunately because our time is limited, we need to move forward, and perhaps if we have more time, we can come back to that. Now, you've told us that from 1992 to date, you've worked at the Ivo Pilar Institute of Social Sciences, and you helped establish that institute in the very beginning; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that is correct. However, I wasn't the only founder. It was a group of Croatian scientists and scholars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer to my question, again, is, yes, you were involved as one of the founders of the organisation. Who were some of the other founders, sir? Let me ask you some -- how about was Miroslav Tudjman one of the founders?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 30 founders, so there was Miroslav Tudjman as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Miroslav Tudjman was one. How about Miomir Zuzul, who has been another witness in this case; was he one of the founders of that institute?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miomir Zuzul was not among the founders of the institute. He was a supporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Jurcevic, your close colleague who testified in this case recently, was Mr. Jurcevic one of the founders of the institute?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also one of the founders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't this institute, sir, at least at the time and for some years, wasn't the institute largely, if not entirely, a defender of or a vehicle for the Tudjman government, sort of to provide the Tudjman government what was seen as "intelligentsia" support?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I categorically state that that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me -- sir, it's no big secret. It happens -- frankly, it happens in the United States as well. We have what some people call think-tanks, and sometimes when you have a Republican administration, there are certain think-tanks that work closely for the government, and when you have a Democrat administration, there are those think-tanks that work closely with that government. And that's what this was, isn't it? The institute was a think-tank, to use my word, it was supposedly the "intelligentsia" to give credence, to give some sort academic intellectual weight to the policies and practices of the Tudjman government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I categorically state that none of those assumptions of yours is correct. The institute, Ivo Pilar, from the beginning was envisaged as a scientific institute in the social development of the area and scientific development. That's how the institute was set up, and today it has international recognition as one such institution. We cooperated with all the various strata in the Croatian society, with the economy, with social institutions, with political institutions. We have broad cooperation, and that we weren't just oriented towards President Tudjman. I can quote one example to bear that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but you've told us already, and in fact Mr. Jurcevic told us the same thing, this is an institute funded by the government, it was founded by people closely -- part of or associated with the government, including the son of Franjo Tudjman, including yourself, including Mr. Jurcevic. You would have been an assistant minister of justice. This was a government operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I have to say, once again, that that isn't correct either. The institute was established on the 18th of November, 1991, on the basis of a decision taken by the Assembly of the University of Zagreb, as a university institution, therefor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't want to raise an objection before the witness was allowed to answer. However, just look at that question asked by the Prosecution. It's pure speculation, because for a question to be asked in this way, you have to know the legal framework in Croatia at that time and how, according to that legal framework, and only according to that legal framework, university institutions and other similar institutions could be established. Now, if the Prosecutor doesn't know that, it's his problem, but he has to ask the witness. Otherwise, this is speculation, which is not permissible, because he wants to put it to the witness that it's a government institution. There is no government institution. That's just not correct, and the witness explained how it was established. I'm not going to take up more time with the cross-examination, although there'd be lots of interesting things to go into there, but that was my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your objection is noted in the transcript. Yesterday, I asked the witness a few questions on the financing of the institute and the appointment of its head, so I did wonder about what the position of this Ivo Pilar Institution was in relation to the Croatian government, which is why I asked all these questions yesterday. But maybe Mr. Scott has something else in mind. I don't know. Let's see where he's going. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Your Honours, to avoid any misunderstanding, yes, that's the crux of it, but you put the question correctly. You didn't speculate and say that it was an institution of this kind or that kind. What you did was to ask the witness directly about certain things and aspects in order to be able to understand what kind of institution it was. Now, my learned friend is speculating. He says it's a government institution. First of all, that did not stem from yesterday's questions, and, secondly, the most important point, it does not follow from the law. If he doesn't know the law, he shouldn't ask, or he should learn the law and then ask. That's my objection. The.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, we don't know whether Mr. Scott had any other questions. Maybe he has other elements, you know, at hand and he would like to demonstrate that this institute is totally dependent on the government. I don't know what he wants to prove, but let's wait and see. But my fellow Judge has questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I would just add to what the President said that we are not so naive as not to know that the legal framework is one thing and the political orientation is another thing, and these are two different matters, and I do not see why the Prosecutor should not be allowed to inquire about the political orientation of this institute, even if formally it's a university institute, it's formally independent and so forth. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll take on board what you've just said, and I agree with what you've said, but let him ask about the political orientation, then. I apologise. Maybe I wasn't clear enough in what I said. All I'm saying is that I object to the way in which the question was formulated, because in the way it was asked, it was a speculation implying a fact that is not correct. Legally, it is not correct, nor is it based on the facts as we've heard them so far. That's my objection. Just look at that question, look at the way it was worded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I think you're slightly overdoing it. We accept that the legal thing is one, but Mr. Scott did not ask about the legal thing, but on affiliation, not legal but of loyalty, and that's a matter which I see no reason to object to. Please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, Your Honours, the question is on the record. Everybody can read it. I'll say no more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your CV, you also tell us that you received a medal and award for the foundation of the institute. When did you receive that medal? All I'm asking for now is a date. You don't need to give me any other explanation. When did you receive the medal?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the medals were distributed by the institute, itself, autonomously to its founder members. I think it was in 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And is it not correct, sir, that a number of people who had been identified previously with the Croatian Ministry of Defence, a section or department that's been frequently referred to in this courtroom as IPD, Information and Propaganda, sometimes someone referred to it as Information and Psychological Operations, those people, people like Mr. Zuzul, Mr. Jurcevic, and others, these were mostly the same people who moved over and were closely involved with the institute; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, several of them took part in the founding, and they took part in 1990 and 1991, when the IPD still didn't exist. So the agreement to found the institute came in 1990, immediately after the democratic elections, and we set into motion the initiative before anybody knew of any IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, again, sir, I mean, I'm not -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, why do you want to take the floor? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] IPD is not propaganda. We've established that a hundred times through the documents. It's Information and Psychological Operations or Activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour, but I'm not going to take the time to deal with it. There's clear evidence in this record about the use of IPD being propaganda. There's been multiple witnesses who have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Be that as it may, sir, and I'm not bashful about using the example of my own government, the United States, there's certain outside groups and governmental agencies, and there evolved a relationship which some people call a revolving door. One day, they're in government, the next day, they're in a closely-related privately organisation, a revolving door, in and out, back and forth, and that was the relationship between IPD and the Pilar Institute, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the Pilar Institute --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, yes or no. I asked you several times. You're not listening to my question, sir. Now, I'm going to get serious about this. We're using time on the clock. My question can be answered yes or no. Was a revolving door relationship -- excuse me, Your Honour. Can I finish my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, listen to the question put to you by the Prosecutor. He wants you to answer by yes or no. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal goes along that line. Even at the Nuremberg trial, this question was amply discussed when the Prosecutor Jackson did not want the witness to answer by making speeches or lectures, and the Nuremberg Tribunal allowed the witness to specify his answer, and Prosecutor Jackson was very unhappy about this. But that's the way it was at the time. However, here the jurisprudence is more restrictive. The Prosecutor puts a question to the witness during the cross-examination, and the witness is supposed to answer by yes, no, I don't know. And if the Prosecutor wants additional information, then he will put another question to the witness, Why are you saying yes, Why are you saying no? And then you can develop, because, remember, the Prosecutor has a limited amount of time and he wants to use it wisely. He is in control of the cross-examination. You are in his hands. Every time you go astray, of course, the Prosecutor will want to put you back on track. So please answer yes, no, I don't know, and if Mr. Scott wants additional information, he will allow you to do so. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can turn in your binder to P11027, P11027. Turn there, please. The Croatian original article, sir, should be behind the translation which I see you have in front of you. Sir, we're not going to have time to go through this article in detail, but basically it sets out this relationship and the involvement of Miroslav Tudjman, Miomir Zuzul, the relationship between all these people, IPD, this institute, and again, sir, that was the relationship, wasn't it? It was closely identified with the Croatian intelligence services; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, that is absolutely incorrect, and this whole article is rampant with lies about the institute, and we denied them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Your position is that it was not. And, in fact, sir, among these various people that we've talked about so far this afternoon, you have worked closely with a number of these people, you have published and otherwise participated in a number of works with the various of -- these same people. In your CV, sir, if I'm not mistaken, you've co-published or been -- participated with Mr. Zuzul in five publications, you've associated yourself with Mr. Jurcevic in five publications, you've written at least one article with Markica Rebic, head of one of the Croatian intelligence services, and by the way, sir, is that the same Markica Rebic who was convicted of contempt by this Tribunal for disclosing the testimony of a protected witness in the Blaskic case? It is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, with all due respect, you have asked me so many questions now that I don't know what you're, in fact, asking me. So can you ask me the questions one by one, and then I'll be happy to answer. This way, you've put forward certain theses and you've actually asked ten questions in one, so you're putting me in an impossible situation. I can't answer like that. There were different people different times, my different knowledge of these people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me summarise it this way: Sir, you were part of a circle of people, and had been for a long time, closely connected to Mr. Zuzul, Mr. Jurcevic, Miroslav Tudjman, Markica Rebic, and a number of other people in that same circle and that colours your world-view and, in fact, reflects your world-view, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I dealt with scientific scholarly activity after 1992. They dealt with other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P11020, P11020. While you're turning to that, sir, I'll just say for the record this is a document put together by the UNPROFOR, the UN Protection Force, as of March 1, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a document prepared by UNPROFOR about the Croatian intelligence and security organisations or hierarchy. If we look at the document, sir, and the drawing, you'll see President Tudjman at the top of the page, you'll see Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Susak, and in the third role on the far left, I think you'll see "Vlado Sakic, director, Institute of Social Research." That's you, isn't is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay, sir. If you look -- and there's a chart as part of that exhibit. If you're at P11020, you should see a handwritten chart, a diagram?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you're on the wrong document, sir, you're on the wrong document. If I could have the usher's assistance. P -- unless I have the wrong number. If I do, I apologise. 11020, on the screen also in front of you. That's you in the box marked "Vlado Sakic"; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I am the head of the Institute for Social Research. I don't know what all this is about, nor has this got anything to do with reality. I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll look, please, at Exhibit P11023 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, UNPROFOR was headquartered in Zagreb, and in March 1994 it drafted a document where it is placing the structure of the Croatian Intelligence Service. Now, maybe they made a mistake, but this is what they believe the structure of this intelligence service was. In this organisational chart, you seem to be part and parcel of the Intelligence Service. And in Chapter C in this document, all these people are mentioned, and you are mentioned under small F. You are mentioned as an expert in analysis and so forth and so on. And Mr. Scott is saying that you are part and parcel of the Croatian Intelligence Service, so do you think that the UNPROFOR made a mistake? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's precisely what I want to clarify. This was written in 1994; right? Counsel, was this written in 1994? When was this written?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as both I have indicated to you and as is stated in the document, and as President Antonetti indicated to you, it was written March 1994.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in 1994, I was not the director for the Institute for Social Sciences called Ivo Pilar. That's the first point. Secondly, the Ivo Pilar Institute was never, throughout its existence, part of any intelligence system, nor did it ever deal with any type of intelligence work. I'm saying that by way of telling the truth, under oath, and the fact that I wasn't actually the director of the institute at that time just shows you the merits of the people who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps I think we should look at this a bit more closely. There are two kinds of relations indicated. Some are indicated with a straight line. That is what actually belongs to the Secret Service. Other relations are broken lines. The relation here to the Social Research Institute is a broken line, which indicates that the meaning of this scheme is not that the institute is a part -- belongs to the Secret Service. And if we look on page -- on top, the number is R0026529, under letter F, it is only said that the institute is linked to the Croatian Information Service. I just want to set this clear. I'm not saying whether this is how it is or not, but the allegations coming from this paper is not that the institute belonged to the Secret Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, nor did he belong to, nor was he linked up with it, and what it says here is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That was not a question I put to you. It's for the Prosecutor to put the questions now. I just wanted to clarify how I interpret the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel, and I agree with that, and I was going to pursue that further. But you've done so, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, with that helpful clarification by Judge Trechsel, this is, indeed, sir -- come on. This is, indeed, the relationship that you had. Maybe you weren't actually inside the Croatian Information Service that Miroslav Tudjman was the head of, but you or the institute, you had a close working link to these organisations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we've finished with this, I'd just like, out of an abundance of caution, to draw your attention to this. This is a UN document, and it says "Confidential" quite clearly there, and it deals with intelligence matters. And as far as I know, that wasn't in its mandate; that is to say, they were forbidden from dealing in intelligence. So I assume that the document could be confidential, so out of an abundance of caution I don't want us to do any harm by using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unnecessary, Your Honour. I don't think there's any big surprise that somebody operating in UNPROFOR at the time would probably like to know who was doing what in various positions of the governments that they were dealing with on a regular basis. I don't think that should come as a surprise to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, in fact the institute --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. [Interpretation] I don't think we have had a ruling with respect to this document's confidentiality. All the documents in this courtroom which come from the UN are confidential, and I see -- I don't see why the question isn't -- the Prosecutor isn't raising the question of this document's confidentiality. I'm wondering what the reason for that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, does this document come under Rule 70 or was it disclosed so you could use it in a public setting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I specifically have not taken a position about confidentiality. I've used it publicly because I don't believe there's any issue about it, and that's our position. I don't know why counsel is so concerned about something where the Prosecution's tendered the document and believes there's no issue about it. If they have some information to the contrary, then we can certainly pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I'd like to come back to is the point, sir, that not only was your institute supporting the Tudjman regime from time to time and closely, but that institute has also been closely involved in providing support to the Defence teams of various accused coming before this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's next turn to P11023, P11023. This is a report from a Croatian government agency, and in the third paragraph it says: "As far as the work with the Defence witnesses of Dario Kordic is concerned, lawyers have emphasised the need to hire social psychologist, whereas M," I believe that's Miomir Zuzul, "has suggested them to address Mr. Vlado Sakic, director of Institute Ivo Pilar, in Zagreb regarding that matter." That was Mr. Zuzul's recommendation that you be retained on behalf of the Dario Kordic Defence team; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I've never heard of this, I never learned of this, nobody told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Zuzul never approached you to work for Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Zuzul never approached me. My contacts with him were very rare at the time, and I would certainly remember if he had spoken to me about that. But since I'm one of the best known social psychologists in Croatia, I can imagine that his proposal was that I should be the expert in the case, just like the Defence has now asked me to be their expert. Zuzul knows it because we went to unit [as interpreted] together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you also know a man named Milan Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Gorjanc, no, it doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll spell it, at least using English pronunciation, G-o-r-j-a-n-c. He apparently is something of a Defence expert, something about dealing with Defence. Did you -- you've never had any dealings with Mr. Gorjanc? Did you know that he was also being put forward at the same time as a witness for Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I've never heard of this person, and I've never heard of him having been put forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to the wording of my learned friend's question, the last one that he put to the witness. It is not clear, from the way the question was put, who could have put forth Mr. Gorjanc as a witness. Maybe this can be clarified to avoid any confusion in this courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, on page 27, line 16, your answer is noted as: "Zuzul knows it because we went to unit together." I suspect that there is a mistake. Can you recall what you said and repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes: It was "university" or "uni."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The interpreters tell me that it was "university" or "uni" as short for "university." Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I don't understand what it says here. We were not in a unit together. We went to university together. And, second of all, I don't know what he knows. I only know that he never invited me. I was never invited by anybody to appear as an expert. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your answer would have been, yes, full stop. I asked you whether it meant "university." Yes would have been the correct answer. Instead, you talk and talk. Please be economic with your words. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to respond to counsel's question and to clarify, it might ring a bell, sir, if you saw the name in print, because maybe I mispronounced something. But if you look at the last paragraph of the document, the same document, P11023, you'll find the passage where it says that: "After this talk, D. Kordic'S Defence lawyers have talked to Milan Gorjanc, potential Defence expert witness - JNA colonel who served in the area of Sarajevo and Central Bosnia," et cetera. So does that refresh your recollection at all about the involvement of Mr. Gorjanc in these matters, or potential involvement?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I didn't have anything whatsoever to do with the Kordic Defence or with Mr. Gorjanc. I don't know who Mr. Gorjanc is. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's move forward to your report and some of the methodology that you employed there. Let me ask you about that in terms of -- as I review your CV, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I -- Your Honours, I apologise. We received these documents before the cross-examination. Maybe the Prosecutor should tell us whether this is only one part of a document. I can see two pages, without any heading and any signature. I don't know what the origin of those two pages is. For the time being, it's very impossible to tell where they come from and what they serve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Prosecutor, P11023, where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was produced to the Office of the Prosecutor, Your Honour, by the Croatian government, from one of the intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not information, this is not a department. The government is huge, it has a number of agencies, 10 ministries, and also the question arises as to the time. But what I'm interested in is whether some part of the material can be identified. We should at least hear the heading of that material, the title of the body. This would allow us to check the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you meet that request, Prosecutor, or don't you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can make further inquiries, as time allows, but the document -- everyone in the courtroom -- everyone in the courtroom has exactly the same document that I have. It says "Info" on the top, at least in translation. It's dated the 22nd of November, 1999. I did research the document to the extent of confirming that it was produced to us by the Croatian government, and that's the only additional information I can provide at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in connection with your report, and I believe you told us yesterday, that you don't have any particular expertise about Bosnia and Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna. I believe you testified yesterday that essentially you knew about these events to the same extent as anyone who might have followed these events in the media at the time would know; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, and I said that I read publications, scientific and others, and that I spoke to my colleagues, scientists and scholars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reviewing your CV, sir, and in the long list that you've provided to us in the publications and the writings that you've done, which are considerable, you have never written an article, for example, on the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, itself, or the creation of Herceg-Bosna, or anything about that, have you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, not directly about Bosnia-Herzegovina. I wrote about the Serb aggression, which encompassed the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Hence, in my papers, you can find information about Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina because it was a one-and-the-same aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: What Herceg-Bosna documentation did you review, preparing your report? If you could just give us a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I said that I had read the scientific publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know, sir, but I just want to -- which Herceg-Bosna documents have you read? Did you read the establishment on 18th of November, 1991? Did you read the meetings of any of the HVO government sessions? Have you read any of the HVO military orders? The answer is, no, isn't it, sir, you've never reviewed a single HVO document; correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, yes, I did read Dr. Jurcevic's expert report, and I'm serious of other --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's exactly what you did, sir, and now you're hopefully maybe saving some time, because what you did, in its entirety, is you relied, for your fact base, if you will, for your fact base, you relied, some of us might say "lock, stock and barrel," on Mr. Jurcevic's expert report prepared for the Defence of Mr. Praljak to give to these Judges, and you took that as gospel, and that's the only thing you've used, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's not true. I have told you that I read other scientific publications, for example, Markesic's book, "How We Saved Bosnia-Herzegovina," and a number of other professional publications and reports on damages that were inflicted on Bosnia and Herzegovina, media reports, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go back, sir, because I'm trying to be fair with you. If you reviewed an HVO document, minutes of the sessions of a meeting of the government presided over by Jadranko Prlic, an order from General Petkovic, who was a chief of the HVO military, if you reviewed any of those documents, just give us one example, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my book, documents and individual events, as a social psychologist, does not have the same significance as it does for a lawyer or a historian. For me, events are important if I can analyse them. I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'm going to cut you off. You heard what President Antonetti told you. Now, I didn't ask you what was significant to you or not significant. My question is a very straight forward one. Give me an example, please, of an HVO or Herceg-Bosna document that you reviewed in connection with your work; give me the order of General Petkovic on such and such a date; give me the minutes of the meeting of the government on such and such a day. Just identify for us, please, one document that you reviewed in connection with your work.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not read any individual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm sorry to interrupt you? I would to ask the witness about the following, which partly comes from your questions, but I also, when I read the document, I found out the following, and I am asking you, Professor, about the very content of your study here and actually the ratio of various major chapters here. If you have a look at the pages, then you will see that you have devoted 10 pages to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 10 pages. On page 2 of the report, 2 and 3 of the report, you will find the pages and the parts of the report, and from page -- the whole report, I'm sorry, the whole report is about 110 pages, including also the references. Now, the part 3 of human aggressiveness and war, it is actually which deals with the war in BH, and the causes of war in BH, 1991, 1995, in the context of the proposed theoretical framework, it starts at 95 and it ends at 105, and all the rest, in my view, quite general. In the first major part, it is the part A, "Socio-psychological Framework Needed for Understanding the War in BiH, 1991-1995," from page 4 to page 60-61. It is then more than 60 per cent of your study. Then the second major part, the application of the socio-psychological framework to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and here we find again a historical background, and you, for example -- what I read again and watched the interesting developments which you refer to of Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1878 up to the end of the First World War, that is at around 40 years, you wrote more about that period of time, and I read it with interest because I am Hungarian. But, on the other hand, it is much more than what you devoted to the question of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1991 and 1995. So my question is that when you wrote this report and when you worked on it, what kind of reasons led you to have those, in my view, rather strange ratio of various parts of the study which I referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my expert report, and you have noticed it well, consists of several parts, but there are basically two main big parts. One is a theoretical apparatus that I have used, and I'm talking about a series of social and psychological theories. I meant that that was the way to best serve this Trial Chamber, to offer it a number of contemporary social theories. And then in the second part, I incorporate relevant factors which had led in two directions. The first one was the establishment of identity groups or war groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the historical period, and the second was an important factor which was the breakup of Yugoslavia, without which I believe nobody can understand what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1992 through 1994. I believe that I would best serve the Trial Chamber in that way; first, to offer a theoretical framework and then, within that context, to say something from the point of view of social and psychological theories, which postulates from those theories can be applied to the general events in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In my expert report, I indicated that the perspective of a social psychologist does not imply this type of facts that the counsel is referring to. All it takes is processes and events which can be incorporated within a certain theoretical framework. If there's a series of such events and if they have their background, social psychology is interested in the causes and consequences, and if there is such a phenomenology, then one is able to produce such an expert report. If the expert report had to be at a lower level, tied to individual events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then I would have said to the person who commissioned the report, Give me some room and I will explain every single event, every single crime, I or some other colleague of mine will produce an expert report based on the same theoretical background, and it will be a particular expert report. My colleague Aronson did that for the incident in Mi Lai.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for your answer. Frankly, I am not convinced. My question remains that if somebody is going to prepare a report on something like the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, five years' war, then it doesn't devote only 10 per cent of everything what he's writing. I, myself, I used to write, and I something know about this material. So I am not convinced, but please, Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just continuing on with some of these questions. You do say in your report -- and in fact one of the things we've been talking about the last hour or so is something what lawyers and judges call bias, and, in fact, sir, and I suppose to your credit, you do admit in your report that you are aware of the bias that you have, and you tell us that you took some steps or tried to take some steps to correct for your own bias. You refer to that on page 65 of the English version and on page 63 of the Croatian language report. You say that you're aware of the possible biases and world-view -- and world-view, and that you, paraphrasing to make it into refer to you, and that you, as a scientist, have tried to minimise their influence. Now, if you tried to minimise their influence, sir, perhaps we could start with you telling us what biases or what world-view do you have that causes you to think that you need to correct for that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, as a scientist, I referred to Weber's principle of neutrality, and I said that as a scientist with a certain cultural background, I shared the fate of all scientists in the world. I have this cultural background bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, sir. But what -- tell us, specifically, though. Don't leave it so vague for the Judges. They have to try to understand your testimony. And in doing so, you've said that you have certain biases and world-views, and just make those explicit, please. Just what bias and world-view do you have that might reflect your work in this case? You apparently thought it was important enough, sir, to put in your report.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Counsel, in order to be fair and objective, I did not say "world-view," but I said my origin, since I am a Croat, and one of the warring parties were Croat, so I simply admitted that, and I said that, as much as I could with the force of my conscience, I made it sure that that cultural background would not influence the objectivity of my expert report. It is very customary in social psychology and in scientific words that the authors state their national background in order to eliminate the fact that value bias does not exist or that they should be neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us, sir, what steps you took. If we can't get it in terms of what your bias is, we can't be more explicit about that, what steps, then, did you take to address that bias?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I believe that I wasn't biased. I used the theoretical apparatus, and I applied the apparatus to general circumstances in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian aggression, and the war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not making this up. I'm referring to your own report, and if you want to turn in your report to page 63 of the -- let me -- I'm trying to save as much time here as possible. If you'll turn to page 65 of the Croatian language version of your report. And for the English readers, if you turn to page 66, which is 3 -- in your report --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your report, for the record, is 3D03721. It was in the Defence material. Let me just read it to you, sir. Please listen. It's very short. And, again, as I've said in the courtroom before, if I say it wrong -- or it's on the screen in front of you. Better yet. It's right on the screen in front of you, sir. Now, it says at the end of that -- on page 66, in the middle paragraph that starts with the words: "In order ...," you say: "In order to reduce any possibility of personal value bias, the author of this expertise has used, in addition to the undisputedly expert review of Josip Jurcevic on the same subject available to the author, the historical perspective of Noel Malcolm, especially in areas that were most sensitive with respect to values." That's in your report, isn't it? That's clearly a yes-or-no answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm just curious, because in the English version, one curiosity. In the English version, you have these words that it says -- let me be very clear. In the English version, it has the words "in addition to the undisputedly expert review of Josip Jurcevic on the same subject available to the author," but in the Croatian language version that language isn't in there, and I'm just curious as to how that discrepancy occurred.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I really don't know how this happened. I, myself, said that I used Josip Jurcevic's expert report, but I don't know how this might have happened. I really don't know. I did not collate the English and the Croatian version at the end when they were finalised, so I really can't tell you how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see. But the reality is, sir, you relied, as I said to you some moments ago, you relied virtually entirely -- you simply took Mr. Jurcevic's report and you relied on that as the factual basis for your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, as I've written, I took him and Noel Malcolm, when it came to value, attitude towards various groups. I took that from Noel Malcolm, and I indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that the clock -- but if I can -- might finish this point with one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I do see that, and I do see the language I pointed you to a moment ago. And you say you used the historical perspective of Noel Malcolm, but, sir, isn't it correct, and the Judges have probably read your -- I'm sure they have, and if we all had time, we could go through all the references, we could go through all the citations to Noel Malcolm, and I put to you, sir, the only time you cite to Noel Malcolm is when you're talking primarily about Bosnia during the Ottoman Empire. Not exactly the core part of your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, historical background was relevant for that chapter, and that's why I used Noel Malcolm the most and also what Dr. Jurcevic wrote. I used the two authors in that chapter. When I needed a historical perspective, I cited historians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that what really happened here, and part of it may be -- some of the mystery may be illustrated by the discrepancy between the English and the Croatian versions, I put to you what happened here is after -- essentially, after you'd completed your report, it occurred to you or someone that just citing Mr. Jurcevic was probably not a great idea, didn't show much balance, but -- so you could salt into your report a few references to Noel Malcolm in connection with the history of the Ottoman Empire; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, of course it's not correct. If that was correct, Josip Jurcevic would be found in Croatian and not in the English version that was sent to the Court. It's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can take the break now, if it's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's a quarter to, and we will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, there's one part of your report that seems to me to be one of the -- probably not the only one, but one of the sections that really kind of goes to the core of what you seem to be saying, and this is from page 88 of the English version. It can also be found on page 85 in the Croatian language, at least just to focus -- I'm not getting anything yet. There we go. Just to give us a focal point. And you'll have it -- I think you'll have it on e-court. But you say, and this is on page 88, English, page 85 of the Croatian, about halfway down through that paragraph: "In accordance with the socio-psychological framework of spontaneous group formation in crisis situations, in addition to collective behaviour, processes of deindividuation appear to a greater extent in which there was a weakening of the usual restrictions and behaviour that opened up possibilities for uncontrolled crimes. Precisely such crimes and on these theoretical foundations, in the main occurred in the conflicts of Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats during 1993 and early 1994. Therefore, in accordance with the provided theoretical framework, is not possible to fully control these processes because, as a rule, they occur spontaneously." Now, the part that I want to focus on at this moment, and we'll see how much time we have to finish these things, but let's focus on spontaneous group formations and the fact that these things occurred spontaneously. It seems to me, sir, that you simply take as a given -- you postulate that Herceg-Bosna and what the Prosecution submits in this case was the pursuit of a Greater Croatia, you just posit that these things were spontaneous, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, this doesn't refer to that, nor is that the case. This refers to the formation of individual groups and not to Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, what we want to talk about this case, I put to you, what the Prosecution wants to put to you, and what the Judges want to know about, is the formation of Herceg-Bosna. That's the group -- that's the group I put to you, and the formation of that group wasn't -- or the operations of that group weren't spontaneous at all, were they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, as a social psychologist, I don't look at the establishment of Herceg-Bosna but the formation of war groups as ethnic groups and ethnocentrism within them, and the war groups of Bosniaks, Croats and so on, and their homogenisation according to ethnocentric principles, I view and look at in reaction to the aggression which came from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if that's the case, you've just defined the core of this issue out of the context -- out of the scope of your report. We're here -- we're here to talk about what happened in this case, not in some theoretical -- not what happened in Tennessee, or Stanford, or somewhere else. We're talking about this case, and you're saying you didn't even consider that what was happening was not spontaneous, but, in fact, highly organised, directed from the top down, and not spontaneous at all. And you just -- are you telling us you just jumped right over that whole point?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, we know that Herceg-Bosna, when it was constituted, was constituted when -- that is to say, when the conflicts started between the Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats, then the two ethnic groups in conflict set up certain institutions as protection. Of course, in that conflict, which was a reaction, once again, to the basic source, so I said clearly that we can ask ourselves whether the conflict would have come about at all had there not been the Serb aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me take you to a few specific examples, sir. When you did your report, when you're preparing a report and concluding that these things were just spontaneous and essentially no one could be held responsible, that there was no plan, did you read the record of a presidential meeting where President Tudjman said: "The solution lies in the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina ...," and where he says that that would be achieved "... because this is equally in the interest of Serbia and Croatia, while the Muslim component has no other exit than to accept the solution"? Did you consider that in forming your views?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I think that there is a misunderstanding, a basic misunderstanding between us. I acted as a social psychologist. I didn't deal with any political frameworks, and that is up to the political science people and historians, not me. I dealt with groups and their homogenisation, and the different groups that were participants in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that's the relevant analysis, because social psychology offers you the possibility of showing how this homogenisation took place which was at the base of the conflict. Had there been no homogenisation, the conflict would have not come about. So I didn't deal with any political documents or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't deal with any political documents. You just decided that the groups you were interested in were some other groups and not the leadership of these organisations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't deal with that. All I dealt with was social psychology and the socio-psychological context, how those groups were formed and how certain leaders can emerge in situations like that. But I didn't deal with the political framework. That wasn't my assignment. It went beyond the frameworks of the nature of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, on page 85 of your report, you titled the chapter "Process of War Group Formation." Very well. It's extremely interesting. And in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a number of people set up the Croatian Council for Defence of the Croatian Community, so a number of persons are going to set up an entity. I believe that for the Judges, for myself and my fellow Judges, for everyone, it would have been very interesting to know what was the psychological or the sociological process which made it possible for a number of people to get together in order to form this group, but I don't feel that this was addressed in your report. Was this deliberate or did you just decide not to attack the problem from this angle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my expert report that is all explained. Of course, individual groups, when they become homogenised, they establish certain institutions. There's no dilemma there. But the process of homogenisation took place before, and we didn't expect there to be a conflict at all between the Bosniak Muslims and the Croats at the beginning of the Serb aggression on Slovenia and Croatia. What was expected, and that's what happened, that if there was a conflict, then the Bosniak Muslims and the Croats would cooperate, collaborate, and that's what happened. However, as the Serb aggression moved from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had a new context, and that's what I write in my report, too, and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina you don't have two ethnical homogenous groups being formed, that is to say, of the Croats and Bosniak Muslims, but they just functioned on a general level; but what was actually being created was within this ethnic corpus many other subgroups and substrata were formed which were homogenised into a third line and on a third level under different situations, and then they become homogenised and without always having common goals. Part of their goals were common goals, but other goals were not common goals. So that's the psychological logic of that process in keeping with the theories of social identity, realistic conflict, that I offered up, and the theoretical apparatus from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, a group is set up of individuals, you agree with me, and these individuals setting up the group or making up the group might make up a homogenous group. I don't know. We know that individuals make up a group, but let me give you a couple of examples in the situation of General Praljak and the situation of a witness we've heard recently, Colonel Skender. According to what we know, General Praljak was an artist in Croatia and then he became a minister for defence. And then he left this eminent position to go and help out in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's one example. Second example. Colonel Skender, legionnaire in the French Army, who was very high ranking for a foreigner because he became lieutenant colonel, and he could have just sat idly in Corsica, taking advantage of the landscape, and what -- he decided to go and join the HVO. So I was wondering what his motivation was. Did he want to integrate a group, did he want to be part of a group? This is the kind of question that we have, and any reasonable Judge must put these questions and could try to find answers to these questions through a report like yours, but your report doesn't seem to answer our concern. So what can you say about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is true that at that level -- that my report does not refer to that level, but from the theoretical context, we can provide a probable answer to questions of that kind as well. Now, I explained the theories of ethnocentrism, of nationalism, the formation of ethnic groups according to socio-psychological criteria, and the principles according to which these groups are formed; religion, culture, language, and common ancestors. That is characteristic for ethnic groups. So when an ethnic group is under threat, then homogenisation within that ethnic group occurs according to those principles, the ones I've just set out, and that's how those ethnic groups come into being in the first place, all those who are similar. And that's the principle of group formation, similarity under crises, those who are similar and have similar characteristics, and they become homogenised and then make up more or less cohesive groups. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation was as follows: The Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats homogenised at a given point in time for two reasons. In the subgroups, there were different ethnic strategies.
