They were never identical on both sides, and I say this in my report, so that because of that, in some places they cooperated, in other places they fought each other, so there wasn't a uniform united, ethnic strategy. But ethnocentrism occurred in both these parts, and in the subgroups, too, and that's the third level of the process of homogenisation. So new contexts were formed and certain events took place. So in answer to what you asked about Mr. Skender and Mr. Praljak, probably both of them arrived according to those principles because they have certain characteristics that link them. Now, as for Mr. Praljak, I don't know. He was in the Ministry of Defence in the Republic of Croatia when cooperation documents were signed with Bosnia-Herzegovina, so probably it was within that context that he cooperated and went to Bosnia-Herzegovina in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, if I understand you correctly regarding this theory of ethnocentrism, it's sufficient to have people that have religion, culture, language and ancestors in common to make up an ethnic group, and if I understand you correctly, the Croatian community which was set up in Herceg-Bosna was set up in this context, people who said, We have a common language, common religion, common history, and because of this we will belong to this group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to those socio-psychological theories, that would then be correct. Religion, language, culture, those are -- and common ancestors, those are the factors, but it's a little different from the establishment of national communities, because with national communities you have to have a nation and a national state, which is a more complex phenomenon, and for ethnic communities and groups, what you said, Your Honour, is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think I somewhat perceive what you're saying. It's quite complicated, but you'll agree with me that it is complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, I read, Witness, on page 46, line 9, the following sentence: "In the subgroups, there were different ethnic strategies." It's a short sentence. In the subgroup, there were different ethnic strategies. You have said that here a short while ago. Could you explain what you mean by this, ethnic strategy in a subgroup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the level of ethnic communities, that is to say, at the level of their organisation, political organisation, of course various decisions were made, agreements reached, and so on. Now, those decisions and agreements were made by those who were in charge, who led those ethnic groups, and of course they tried to apply that to all the ethnic groups, entire ethnic groups. However, because of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I've spoken about that several times already so I don't want to repeat myself, it was difficult to implement that because many subgroups were formed due to the objective conditions prevailing in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the separation within the same ethnic corpus due to the wartime conditions and other factors. However, in those groups and subgroups, of course, you had discussions and debates, and in each of the ethnic groups the principles were followed of the ethnic group to which you belonged, to which one belonged, rather than agreeing to other principles. However, certain strategies were formed within the subgroups, at the level of the subgroups, which, in the socio-psychological context, as I write in my report, frequently did not need to have any points in common, anything linking them to those general principles or decisions. And so those are the spontaneous situations that I refer to, and those norms in those groups are then established by a leader or a group of individuals, and that happens under wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's return to these groups where the Prosecutor got interrupted. I wonder what you have in mind by these groups that are the result of spontaneous group formation. Was it the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it wasn't the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it -- was it criminal gangs like the one known as Kinder Platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, yes, criminal gangs do come under that category. But not only criminal ones, but they were based on other principles too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Scott. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I'm getting French translation on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters are sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to the other groups, and I don't think, sir, and I'll put to you, you can't simply skip over and choose the groups you want to talk about or you've already started your entire work with a conclusion in mind. The group I want to talk about is the leadership group, if you will. And you said leaders come into existence, and the leader I want to talk about are people such as Franjo Tudjman, Mate Boban, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic. That's the group I want to talk about, and you can't just simply skip over them like they don't exist, sir. Now, when you concluded -- you said a moment ago, by the way, that there was no initial anticipation of conflict with the Muslims, but, sir, the quote that I read to you from President Tudjman some minutes ago now, about the need for a partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the fact that the Muslims would simply have to go along, sir, that was June 1991. It wasn't 1993, it wasn't 1994; it was June of 1991 that Mr. Tudjman said that. Now, did you also -- and you talked about homogenisation of groups. When you consider that part of your report, did you read -- did you read part of the record of a meeting on the 27th of December, 1991, where Boban says that by cleansing the border areas of Herceg-Bosna, that would create about 65 per cent of the Croat population in Herceg-Bosna? Did you consider that in your process of homogenisation? Yes or no, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, again I claim that I did not take political decisions into consideration, and I told you why. I was talking about the process of creating groups, conflict among groups, and from that point of view I'm saying whether it was possible to organise something, something to the effect of -- if any kind of organisation was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm talking about the organisation of Herceg-Bosna, and you know full well the role that Herceg-Bosna played in these events. That's the organisation -- that's the group formation that I want to talk about. And you're saying you just skipped over -- you just kind of skipped over that, that wasn't convenient to you to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm not avoiding anything. I am just not dealing with the functioning of political institutions at the time. I'm dealing with the social and psychological aspects of a process to form war groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What you're not dealing with, sir, is the facts of this case. You can talk about theory all you want. We can sit here all day and read textbooks about social psychology. We have to apply it to the facts of this case. Now, did you read -- when you did that, did you read the report by Milivoj Petkovic dated the 26th of June, 1992, where he says that the HVO goal, I emphasise the word "goal," is to put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities, including Mostar and Stolac, and to establish Croatian rule over all municipalities? Did you consider that document in doing your work?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, just a moment. Could you please wait, sir? This is the third or fourth time that my learned friend is asking a question of the witness as to whether he read any other documents, and he puts all of the documents out of any context. This expert's task was to come up with an expert report that was commissioned by the General Praljak Defence team, and the expert moved within that framework. He has repeated several times that he did not deal with the facts of this case. And now the Prosecutor chooses, among the tens of thousands of documents that are already in evidence -- [In English] Would I be please allowed to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Tomanovic, we're all trying to make a wise use of time. What you're saying, you know, the Judges know it fully well. The Prosecutor is putting questions, and the witness is answering, and then the Trial Chamber will draw its own conclusions. Don't think that the Judges are naive or fools. You know, they understand. They understand what's going on. You don't have to warn the Judges, you know, to be careful. It's pointless. If the Prosecutor wants to waste his time, let him waste his time. If he wants to repeat the same question three times, the witness said he didn't see the document, and the Prosecutor is still pressing on, let him do it. Now, regarding substance, you might be right. The expert report was not dealing with the subject. It's obvious. This was a psycho-sociological report and not a report on facts or politics. But if Mr. Scott wants to use his time on this, let him do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I largely agree, and I think that the objection ought to be sustained because the witness has made it very clear that he has not read any document of what is a document in the sense we use the word here, and therefore I think it's really a question that should not -- the kind of question that should not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. [Interpretation] Let me take another 30 seconds of your time. Given the fact that Mr. Scott mentioned the name of my client, and in case any of the documents relative to my client are used, I'm going to refer to the decision on the adoption of guide-lines for presenting a Defence case, guide-line number 1, and I'm going to ask to cross-examine this witness, and I rose only to save some time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I take on board and I take it that much of my task is accomplished and we've established clearly that this witness does not and did not deal with the facts of this case. That was exactly the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The problem is, sir -- the problem is your report doesn't pretend to be -- it doesn't purport to be simply a setting out of theories. You say that these things actually happened. You assert that people in the HVO were out of control. You assert that people who committed crimes were out of control. You just simply -- you don't say these were theoretical possibilities. You say that's what happened. And what I'm putting to you, sir, you can't possibly say that because, as we've just established, you didn't study the facts of this case, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it's suffices for me to read facts that I found in other publications. That's how Aronson did his analysis of Mi Lai, and that was enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So relying on Mr. Jurcevic's report was enough for you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And many others, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going to go back to that point at this point. All right. In light of the comments from the Chamber, let me not take more time on that. Let's turn to a part of your report where you talk about the use of symbols and heroes and values. If you'll go to -- in your report, which the report, for the record, is 3D03721, you talk about -- for instance, on page 6 of the English version, on page 6 and 7 of the Croatian language of the document, you talk about a system of values, culture, and identities, and you refer to something called the "onion diagram," which is then on the page 7 of both the English and the B/C/S versions, and there's a chart there on the middle -- or a diagram on the middle of the page, and you have values, practices, rituals, heroes, symbols. Do you see that -- well, you're familiar with that, aren't you? Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now I'd like to refer you to another exhibit in talking about this topic, and that is P11024, P11024. And there are other parts of this document that if we had time we might get to, but I need to go right now, specifically, to -- excuse me, pages 8 and 9 of your article. There's only one -- let me just read it to you, because there's only one specific part for now that I want to deal with. You say that, in talking about Serbian volunteers, in that paragraph -- it starts on the top of page 9 of the -- or continues over the top of page 9 in English: "Besides, he was the one who awarded Seselj the military title of Chetnik," "duke" is the translation, "and this actually created a symbolic continuity in Serbian, fascistic, and imperialistic territorial pretensions to Croatian territory." Can you tell the Judges what you meant in this article when you described this as symbolic continuity?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm answering questions pertaining to my expert report. How can I artificially establish a link between one document and another and compare them? I can talk about the Chetnik movement, how it developed, and what were its reflections, what its reflections still are, but I cannot establish a link between my expert report and one of my professional papers that I presented as a symposium of the Association for Victimology and that I published in a book of papers that was edited by Dr. Separovic, the vice-president of the World Victimology Society that was organised in Croatia. I really can't understand your question, and it really defies reason, I might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you've told us all sorts of concepts about individuation and group behaviour and conformism, so just tell us, what do you mean when you use the term "symbolic continuity"?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Again, I don't understand your question. You have to tell me what context I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it's your document. I read it to you just now. You're referring to the Serbs and their involvement in this conflict. You say -- I took you to your report where you talk about the role of symbols, heroes, rituals and values. I showed you another document which you've confirmed that you wrote in which you talk, in the context of the Serbs, about the symbolic continuity in Serbian and fascistic, et cetera. Now, I don't have to explain to you, sir, your own work. You don't know what you meant when you said -- used the words "it showed a symbolic continuity"? That has no meaning to you, your own words?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, sir, I don't know my expert report by heart. That's why I wanted to know about the context. However, when you say "symbolic continuity," I incorporated that into the so-called diagram -- arch-diagram, and this is something that is used in anthropology, sociology, and it goes from anthropologic to sociologic to psychological perspective, and that's how I try to incorporate to show that there was symbolic continuity, because the Chetnik movement is an organisation which was illegitimate in the first Yugoslavia, and then the continuity was interrupted in the second Yugoslavia. However, Prince Djues [phoen], who was a Chetnik and who cooperated with Italians and fascists, and he participated together with him in the Second World War, he, in a symbolical way, handed over that duty to Vojislav Seselj, together with the title of "vojvoda," and that's when the Croatian aggression against -- when the Chetnik aggression against Croatia started, and that's how the Chetnik movement continuity -- continues within the framework of the Serb aggression against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I can't ask any questions because I am the Presiding Judge in the Seselj case, I'm not allowed to ask questions, so I have to put this on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's go to some other symbology. And if I could ask you to turn to Exhibit P10522, P10522. Sir --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I might have some -- I'm told it's not in the binder for some reason, so I -- I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at the overhead -- or, excuse me, on the screen in front of you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can just -- if we can just for the purposes of everyone orienting themselves to this document, if you could go to the next page, Mr. Registrar? Oh, it is in the binder, I'm told. I'm sorry. Can you go to the next page ? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, these are all images from the World War II independent state of Croatia. If you go to the next document -- the next page, please. Let's stop on that one for a moment, because that's the one -- because our time is so limited, that I want to focus on. This is a photograph of Jure Francetic, and he has a big U on his helmet, and that stands for "Ustasha," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so. I don't know what Jure Francetic looks like. Now I see him and I can see his name depicted, so I believe you, that it is indeed Mr. Jure Francetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Francetic, in fact, was one of the most notorious Ustasha war criminals of World War II, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what values -- what symbols do you think are communicated when Mr. Francetic is made a hero and one of the HVO units, in fact the unit that some of the people in this case attended the swearing-in ceremony, when an HVO unit is named the Jure Francetic Brigade, what value, what symbol, what message, does that communicate in group formation?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't know. I don't see a link between that and my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us you want to talk about group formation, and you've talked in your report -- and I've taken you to the page where you talk about the importance of symbols, heroes, values. When we have an HVO unit -- the Chamber knows this evidence, they've seen the video of a swearing in ceremony, and it was the Jure Francetic Brigade. What kind of message do you think it sends to the members of that brigade to have their unit named after a notorious war criminal? Come on, you're the social psychologist. You can answer that.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I am not justifying this. If I had participated in that, I would have told them not to call the unit Jure Francetic. And I said it very clearly in my expert report, what my views were -- are of the extremist political organisation known as Ustasha that existed during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, you did not answer the question. The question was: What is the message that this name for the brigade conveys? The answer was not whether you agree or anything of that, but what is the message that is conveyed if a brigade is called after Francetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the message is clear. The message is implied. A link was being established between the independent state of Croatia and the Croatian Army at that moment. I really am not familiar with this unit. I don't know when and where it was formed. But the message, however, is obviously clear, the message of those who created that unit, so there could be no avoiding the link between that unit and the troops -- the army that existed in the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is there any proof for what the counsel is claiming? The messages are clear. I know what he is aiming at, and I provided my answer. However, I don't know whether -- I don't know, I don't know what this is all about. I'm simply confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're now asking a question of me. You ask for evidence that may be in the possession of the Prosecutor. He shows you a photo. I'm seeing it for the first time, myself. We can see a person who seems to be called Jure Francetic. He is in a black uniform. He wears a soldier's helm with a U on it, and the Prosecutor asked you whether it says -- it means "Ustasha," and you say, Yes. And he tells you that there was a brigade with the name of Francetic, did you know that or not? He's asking you what is conveyed by this symbol. That's all. And you said, in your answer, that you would not have used the name. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go on, please, to Exhibit P04020, P04020. This is an order dated the 8th of August, 1993, over the name of Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Briefly, sir, I'd like to direct your attention -- the courtroom's attention to paragraphs 2, paragraph 3, and paragraph 4, and in several -- in those three paragraphs, sir, the document refers to Muslims with the -- what we've come to know a derogatory term called "balijas." "Balija," in the second -- in paragraph 2, "balija" in paragraph 3, "balija" in paragraph 4. Now, what value or symbol or message does that convey, when a commander uses ethnically derogatory language in the orders to the troops under his control, under his command?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the social and psychological logic does not apply to the chapter that you are quoting. You're not privy to the theoretical and methodological apparatus, and I understand that that's why you're putting things into a wrong context. But let me put things in the right context, and let me then interpret things. This belongs to the context of -- of prejudice, as we know them in the socio-psychological context. In a socio-psychological context, this belongs to the way -- prejudices are created towards external groups, and those prejudices are particularly developed in extreme and crisis situations, and they develop very fast. This happened during the war, during the conflict between Bosniak Muslims and Croats. The cognitive part of any prejudice is a stereotype. What stereotype achieves is the process of generalisation applied to all members of a group, based on the same characteristics, and no differences are recognised as existing within that group. And in that logic, a stereotype actually leads to the behavioral part of a prejudice, which is discrimination, and ultimately conflict. One of the stereotypes which were applied in referring to Bosniak Muslims during the war was obviously the stereotype of "balija." This is the same as if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please. Microphone for Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, for the record, I'd just like to make an objection from the Petkovic Defence. We didn't want to influence the witness in his answer, but I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that my learned friend Mr. Scott erroneously interpreted this document, because in that document it is not the Muslims that are being referred to, that is to say, members of an ethnic group, but about an enemy army. I say that so that we can understand the use of this term, regardless of its positive or negative connotations, better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to move forward, sir, to another part of your report. I think you'll find it on page 85 of the Croatian version, but I believe it's on page -- I may have written the page down wrong. You make this assertion in your report, and it says: "Taking into account that many subgroups were not under any institutional control and that possibilities of sanctioning any deviation in the Law of War were minimal or none, according to theoretical framework it is obvious that commanders at various levels could hardly and often not at all fully control the war situation and behaviour of these subgroups." Now, this comes back to the issue that I raised with you a few minutes ago, sir. The problem here is that you don't simply say that your report is a collection -- essentially a textbook on concepts. You say that's what happened. You say that they were not under control. What do you base that on? Who told you they were not under control?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the events that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina were publicised in the media, on television. I said I read publications, I read expert reports. There are sufficient sources for this socio-psychological logic. But this is an application of a theoretical framework to the real situation. It was a spontaneous organisation of groups that I spoke about yesterday, and we repeated that several times today. So it's within the context of conformity, conforming --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you just did it again, though, you make the assertion. It's one thing for you to comment, and I understand if you want to come in and give the Judges a lecture on various concepts, the area that you're involved in, in terms of social psychology. But the problem, sir, and I put to you again, the problem with your report is it purports to go beyond that and say, Well, I'm not talking about theory; I'm talking about what actually happened. You're saying here "were possibilities of sanction" -- "subgroups were not under control. Possibilities of sanctioning were minimal or none. Under these circumstances, they could not fully control the war situation." You don't say those were possibilities. You're telling these Judges that that's exactly what happened on the ground, and then you turn around and tell us, Well, I didn't look at the actual documents. So are we back at saying again: You didn't actually look at the facts of this case, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, no, we seem to be going round in circles here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at Exhibit P03019. And I'm going to show you, as quickly as possible, about four exhibits, and then I'll put a couple of questions to you, so I'll appreciate your cooperation. P03019.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P03019. Sir, the first one I want to show you is, if you have 3019 in front of you, this is an order dated the 30th of June, 1993, over the name of Milivoj Petkovic. I'm directing your attention to paragraph number 8, second sentence. Paragraph numbered 8: "Isolate all able-bodied men in Muslim-inhabited villages in your area of responsibility and leave women and children in their houses or apartments." And then we have this, and I'm going to come back to this, I'm going to ask you and the courtroom to focus on this, and the number of this order we have -- for simplicity's sake, I'm going to focus on the last digits just so we have to repeat fewer digits in the courtroom, but it's 1244/93, you'll see that in the number above, the last part being 1244/93. And then you'll see -- under Petkovic's name, you'll see that the operative zone commander, which is the level of the HVO military hierarchy immediately below Mr. Petkovic, the operation zone commander, Mr. Lasic, sends it on below to brigades under his command, including the 2nd Brigade and the 3rd Brigade. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you'll go to Exhibit P03128, it should be just close by the one you looked at, 3128. This is another order dated the 2nd of July, 1993, a couple of days later. It is over the name, again, of Mr. Petkovic, and indicating "in agreement, Bruno Stojic." And the number on the top of this order is, and the last, again, the last digits, 1259/93, 1259/93. And, again, we have a series of orders going down to various units. I'll note for the Chamber in terms of some recent questions, the involvement of Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, the Tuta ATG, the orders and giving directions to military police units, the order to -- in item number 3, the defence of the town of Mostar, commanders Brigadier M. Lasic, et cetera. You have that order, and I'll ask you, sir, to keep that number in mind, 1259/93. If you go to Exhibit P03117, P03117, the very front, I believe -- right in front of the last one, this is an order dated the 2nd of July, 1993, by Mr. Miljenko Lasic, the operative zone commander, the same day, 2nd of July, 1993. P03117. And Mr. Lasic says, in the first paragraph: "On the basis of General Staff/Main Staff order" and we see "1259/93," which is the document we were just looking at, and Mr. Lasic relays -- sends the order down his chain of command. Among other things, he appoints a military police officer as the sector commander, an order by Mr. Lasic to a military police officer, but we see the reference to 1259/93. Mr. Lasic sends it to the 2nd Brigade, the 3rd Brigade, the 3rd Military Police Battalion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, please really slow down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the last one, before I put a couple of questions to you, is P03156. This is an order the next day, 3 July 1993: "Pursuant to the order of the General Staff number 1259/93," and then also the reference of his immediate commander, Mr. Lasic, "3822/93," then Mr. Broljic [phoen] makes his order to his units. Now, all these have to do, sir, with the arrest of Muslim men -- among other things, the arrest of Muslim men in the first part of July 1993. Don't those documents indicate to you, sir, these were not random, spontaneous acts, were they? Were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, once again there's a misunderstanding here. You're talking about the wartime context, that is to say, orders within the wartime context and facts that I have no reason to doubt that they're as said, and you link that up with something that cannot be linked up. It's got nothing to do with the formation of ethnic groups on a wartime principle. All it has to do with here is with -- with all the war operations. Now, as I say, as I've said several times, I don't have an insight into that area and so can't comment on it, and I can't incorporate it into the theoretical model that I offer up, nor is this at the level of an expert report, the level and assignment I was given. So I would have to analyse all this separately, all these documents that you've put before me, and then, on the basis of that analysis, I would be able to offer up a social-psychological answer. But this is the first time I'm encountering all this. You've quoted a series of orders which you say are linked up in one way or another, but I was not able, rationally, to follow that attentively enough because I don't know the subject matter, so it's impossible for me to answer, although I have the best will in the world to answer. But I cannot answer or incorporate it within the context that I was talking about. There's no theoretical -- this cannot be placed in the theoretical framework which I offered because it's quite a different subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but for the transcript I'd like to say that it would be proper -- I've waited for the witness to finish his answer first, but it would be proper to ask the witness whether he knows what happened in the area on the 30th of June, because if these orders are being placed in some kind of context, one must know how they were engendered. But I think the witness has already answered that in his own way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, in your report you state that there are some rogue groups, uncontrolled groups. Very well, we can read it. And the Prosecutor is using documents to show you that a number of facts occurred after orders were given, after a succession of orders were given. This is the month of July, early July. There are problems between the Muslims and the HVO, so we can't understand what is happening. But it seems that a number of orders were given to isolate Muslims, isolate, arrest, detain. We're not going to go into this. And the Prosecutor did use the word "isolate." Now, he would like to know whether the conclusions of your report actually took into account situations where things did not happen randomly, where things happened after orders had been given. That's the crux of the problem. And given these kind of orders --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you had known, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had known that these orders existed, would you have written the same conclusions in your report or would you have changed your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this part is -- can be incorporated into the part where I say that after the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, that certain crimes occurred on both sides, there were crimes committed on both sides, so I put that in context and said that that was -- well, I said what the cause was and what the consequence was, but I said at the end -- in my conclusions, I put this in a sort of qualitative/quantitative ratio of the crimes committed by the Serbs, as the aggressors leading to the Bosniak Muslim conflict, and I said there was a conflict between these two groups, but from the socio-psychology aspect, you can't ascribe the same responsibility to everyone, given the context. So that's the overall context that I place this in, if we're dealing with an event which was deemed a crime. But, once again, as I say, I'm not clear on these individual situations. I don't know what all this is about. I don't know what the war context is or what the consequences were, so I would have to be informed of all that and then I could answer within the context of my analysis. Of course, you can answer this question, but I can't do it like this, off the bat, because I don't know enough of the facts, I don't know the whole scope or context of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you also say, in the part that I quoted to you a moment ago, that there were no measures -- essentially, there were no measures. It is obvious that commands at various levels could hardly or often not at all fully control the war situation and behaviour of these subgroups. Now, at the risk of getting the same answer and getting further direction from the Chamber, but on this specific topic I'm going to again ask you: Did you review any documentation as to the disciplinary measures available to the HVO, the implementation of disciplinary measures? Did you review any documents where a commanding officer disciplined any of his troops for improper behaviour, or do you -- again, you just simply assert that they were out of control, but you don't really know?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, no, I didn't, and I didn't take that logic. I saw that the commander had very restricted possibilities, and the way in which -- I addressed the way in which these groups were formed very hastily. And as they were mostly volunteers, as the volunteer principle existed, then sanctions and punishment and disciplinary measures didn't exist in the same way as a commander would have with an ordinary army and ordinary soldiers, and so control wasn't possible as of the kind we know in highly-civilised societies and organised armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, sir. And I apologise to the interpreters, but if I just wait until the answer -- until Mr. Sakic stops talking, we spend too much time, I apologise for that. But, sir, I'd like you to look quickly, please, at P02595, P02595? While you're finding that -- do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I expected it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 2595. And while you're looking at that, so I can save time, this is a record of an order by Mario Cerkez, dated the 1st of June, 1993, and in this document Mr. Cerkez, as the brigade commander, takes disciplinary measures against one of his soldiers in the form of a redeployment. Under the order, it talks about the individual's name, it says: "... against whom disciplinary measures were not undertaken in the past, will suffer the following consequences due to his violating the disciplinary rules;" et cetera, and then the first item under that, he is being redeployed from the Batiska [phoen] Brigade to the line of defence. So that's one example I wanted to show you. Would you please look at Exhibit P02650. It should be the next -- very next document, sir, P02650. This is an order a few days later on the 6th of June, 1993, also by Mario Cerkez, about the disciplinary measures taken against the soldier, Bosnjak, and in this instance, in fact, it indicates that while Mr. Bosnjak was originally ordered to spend seven days in detention for a disciplinary violation, Mr. Cerkez sees fit to reduce it from seven days to two days. Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please go to Exhibit P11033, P -- second to last, P11033. Would you agree with me, sir, that another way of controlling behaviour is to -- not only discipline them, in the sense of sending them to detention, but also to remove or relieve people of their position or responsibilities? You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that could be one possible measure. I don't know what act was perpetrated, because it's out of context. You keep wanting me to say something about individual cases, whereas I have no knowledge of the context, and I keep repeating the same thing. I can't give an answer if I don't know the context, but I can look at it from the context of analysis. What would happen had all these soldiers left the unit at that time, all of them? Would there have been any sanctions? If they were to leave the army, would the commander be able to take any disciplinary measures against them?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You got that wrong. I didn't ask you, in any of these situations, to address the facts. I didn't ask you what these soldiers did to deserve the punishment. I didn't. I'm talking about concepts and measures here. And you did agree with me a few moments ago that removing an officer, removing someone, would be another way of sanctioning behaviour, and in P11033, dated the 5th of July, 1993, a decision by Mr. Stojic, we have Mr. Stojic relieving from duty the assistant commander for security in the Stjepan Radic Brigade; correct? "Mr. Dodic has been relieved of duty." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether this document is correct? I see that that's what it says there, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm asking you do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when were --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, sir, I'm forced to ask you --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- when you conclude and you tell these Judges in your report, you didn't say it was just a possibility, you said there were no measures available. Did you review documents like this to see if what you said was true or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm just talking about a general situation where you have volunteers and where people leaving groups and units was not sanctioned. I wasn't speaking about the internal setup or internal relations within individual units and the possibility of taking certain disciplinary measures, so I didn't deal with the military political aspects of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again we'll certainly let the Judges read your entire report and all the assertions you made about the lack of disciplinary measures, and they'll certainly draw their own conclusions about that. Now, I'm going to come back to the topic of in looking at the behaviour, group behaviour, and certainly I think we have to be able to agree that your report deals with group behaviour, did you study and consider the role of the leadership of these groups in relation to group behaviour?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I dealt with it in -- as concerns that part relating to group decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the group decisions made by Herceg-Bosna, did you study those?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I didn't deal with group decisions in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my colleague, but while he continued his examination I checked this out. The document, 11033 that he called up and that we have in our binder, which is also on our screens, has absolutely nothing to do with Mr. Bruno Stojic, and I would just like to have that established. It's the Osijek Military District, the Croatian Army, and has nothing whatsoever to do with Mr. Stojic. I think that my learned friend might have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I had noticed that. Maybe you made a mistake in the number you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I probably did, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I probably did, Your Honour, and I thank counsel for bringing it to my attention. I'm sure it was my mistake. I think the correct number should have been P03186, I hope, if the usher can pull it up on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I apologise if that is the case. I wasn't clear. When the witness answered, he was looking at P11033. That's the document he was looking at in his response. So in view of that correction, I think we should verify that, because this is a document from Croatia, and in his expert report this witness does not talk about Croatia. He doesn't say that disciplinary measures were not possible in Croatia. This is the end of 1993, so that's one thing, and the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina is quite a different matter. So I think that Mr. Scott will have to go back to the document and ask his question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please put your question again to the witness, but when we have the document on the screen, only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll come back to it, Your Honour. I don't think we'll be able to finish before the break, although we're getting close, but if I can come back to it. No need for Mr. Kovacic to talk about what was happening in Croatia. I intended to show a document, and I do have in front of me, the 5th of July, 1993, by Mr. Stojic. Apparently I've written the wrong number on it. I will make efforts to find it and put it to the witness, Your Honour. But before the break, unless the Court would like to take the break now and then we can come back to it? Makes no difference to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. You have 18 minutes left, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't think, to be honest, this is going to change any of the testimony, because I think the answers will be the same, but to be clear, and I apologise for having the number wrong myself, I had simply wrote it on my outline, it was nobody else's fault but mine, the correct number is P03186, P03186. It should be available to everyone now. It's also on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I referred, sir -- just so you know that I was not trying to misdirect you, but when I referred to an order dated or a decision dated the 5th of July, 1993, by Mr. Stojic, removing Mr. Dodik from duty, this is the document I was referring to, if you have that now. Do you have P03186? It's loose on top. It should be -- I think I see it right there next to you there, sir. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so record is clear, that doesn't change your testimony. You say that you did not consider this or the other documents I've shown you, in terms of the potential measures that were available to officers and commanders of the HVO, in terms of disciplining or sanctioning behaviour, does it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, because it did not fit either in the methodology or in the gist of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, I would like to object. This document does not show any link whatsoever. This is a decision on disciplinary measure. It doesn't show that this person was removed from his position because of something that was not admissible. This is just an administrative document, and we don't see why this was done, and we can only see whose proposal it was. This is a document to dismiss somebody from his duties and has nothing whatsoever to do with any disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we -- we need to come back for the purposes of the record and clarify that. But now that we've done that, I'd like to go back to the last topic that we were on before we got to that point. And I did ask you, specifically, if you had studied the role of the -- the role of the leadership of Herceg-Bosna in decisions and the behaviour of Herceg-Bosna, and you indicated that you had not. And I'm looking at the transcript today, page 70 to 71. Sorry, I'm getting a lot of interference. And you indicated on page 70 to 71: "No, no, I didn't, I didn't deal with group decisions in Herceg-Bosna." Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deal with any form of decision-making, with any political or military decision-making processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina or in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure that that was clear. I apologise to Your Honours. I'm just, for some reason, I'm getting a lot of interference in my headset. Sir, I'd like to turn to the last topic in the last few minutes that we have. You've talked in your report about the role of, what you, perhaps at some points called criminal elements or extremist. But rather than these people being out of control, do you allow, sir, for the possibility that they were being used, they were doing exactly what people around them, various military and political leaders, wanted them to do, or did you not consider that scenario?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I already said that to the Trial Chamber. I said that during the Serbian aggression, some groups were used and their leaders were criminals, with criminal files across the globe. Those groups were instrumentalised and used with the purpose of aiding the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean, sir, when you say they were instrumentalised?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that when such groups and when criminals are instrumentalised, they accept to participate in such actions because they know that the real reasons for their participation, looting and the acts of violence which have nothing whatsoever with war goals, will not be punished. Whatever they steal will belong to them. Criminal groups are anti-social and asocial groups, and their primary goal is always personal gain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you would agree with me, wouldn't you, sir, that in terms of a concept, and you told us this afternoon repeatedly that you're dealing often with concepts and not the actual facts, but conceptually there's nothing that would make that phenomenon, if you will, unique to the Serbs? The Muslims could do that, the Croats could do that, various criminal elements could be instrumentalised, to use your term; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, of course it is possible in every military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us, before I go to my couple of final questions, who was Vice Vukojevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I know Vice Vukojevic from the late 1990s as an MP in the Croatian Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't he widely regarded in the 1991-1995 period, and perhaps even still today, as a Croat nationalist of a rather extreme sort?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I can't confirm this. I can't answer your question, I'm afraid. Could you perhaps ask me a somewhat clearer question? What do you mean? Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us all day now and all day yesterday about your extensive work in these areas. You've been at the institute for the last 17 years. We've heard extensively about your connections, the network of people that you've been associated with. In all that time, in all those contexts, you're telling the Judges you've never heard, in any discussion or conversation, or read any media article, that describes Mr. Vukojevic as an HDZ hard-liner, a Croat nationalist who was very close to Minister of Defence Susak?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, then ask me that. Are you saying that the media -- or are you asking me -- or maybe you should ask me about the media and whether I read such articles in the media. I read it in the media, that that's how he was treated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll settle for that for the time -- for purposes of the time. My first question was to you was he was -- not what your view was, but was he widely regarded as, and I think you've just answered that question. Sir, can I ask you to turn to P07695, P07695, about the middle of the binder. This is a record of a presidential meeting on the 27th of January, 1994, and I'd like to direct your attention -- and the page number will be the same in both the English and the Croatian version, page 6 -- starting on page 16. And perhaps in dealing with this, you can remind us -- the Judges, please, who was Dr. Franjo Greguric as of -- in January -- what position did he hold in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't know what his position was. I believe that he was prime minister, but I don't know whether he was prime minister in 1994. He was prime minister in 1992, during the Government of Democratic Unity, and I don't know for how long that government was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sometime around this period of time in the mid-1990s, Mr. Greguric was prime minister of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Objection. [Interpretation] The witness said it clearly, that he didn't know about that time. It was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think the question was -- I wasn't specifically saying -- he said he wasn't sure if it was in January of 1994. I simply came back to allow, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sometime during this period, sir, in the early 1990s, 1992, 1994, Mr. Greguric was prime minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so. I don't know. I can't see it from the document, and I did say that I didn't -- don't know for how long he was prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, he was prime minister at some point in the mid - in early 1990s, sir; yes or no? Come on.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know, I've already told you. He was the prime minister in the Government of Democratic Unity. I don't know for how long. There were ten prime ministers in Croatia in the early 1990s, and it never occurred to me to memorise the dates when they were prime ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when Mr. Greguric was meeting with Mr. Tudjman on the 27th of January, 1994, and I'm going to about the middle of page 16, Greguric says to Tudjman: "I must tell you, Mr. President, I will no longer even share the bench with Vico Vukovic." And I think that's a miss, but you'll see later in the context the full name. I think there's a misspelling of the name. Mr. Greguric and Mr. Tudjman are having this conversation, and then President Tudjman responds, at the bottom of page 16: "Yes, but we cannot finish it without Vice Vukojevic. How do you fail to grasp that? Vice Vukojevic, too, went to Herzegovina where the borders of the Croatian state are being determined." Sir, isn't that an example of what I put to you earlier, what you said in the context of someone being instrumentalised? President Tudjman knew there were objections about Mr. Vukojevic, but responds specifically to Mr. Greguric, Yes, but we can't do the job without him, to that effect, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask my learned friend Mr. Scott to assist us with the transcript, because if I'm following the developments in the courtroom well, then this sentence refers to three people, Vice Vukojevic, Jozo Manolic, and Stipe Mesic. Would you please be so kind and confirm this? Or maybe we're all misreading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. I thought I'd been clear that starting on the bottom of page 16: "President: --" Well, let's go back -- and given what's been said, let's go back to the end of what Mr. Greguric says to put this in further context. I was trying to save time. I apologise: "Those men are in the hospital and external appearances are deceiving, you know, cars. Everything looks good. We've become terribly impoverished. They don't money and are dissatisfied. A host of people have come to me and said, The situation is difficult. The war should be ended. The sooner it ends, the better it will be. There is no other way." "President: Yes, but we cannot finish it without Vice Vukojevic. How do you fail to grasp that? Vice Vukojevic, too, went to Herzegovina, where the borders of the Croatian state are being determined." That's what I read. Now, if counsel wants to read further down the page, Mr. Tudjman, in fact, does indeed confirm that if he could, he would get rid of Mr. Vukojevic, but he just said: "I can't, I need them because of the war. I would get rid of Vukojevic and Manolic and Mesic for other reasons, I would point out, if you read the entire transcript, "I would get rid of them but I need them because of the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to my question, sir. Isn't this an example of someone like Mr. Vukojevic being "instrumentalised" to get the job done?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, based on what I'm reading, I can't answer your question. I can't find any context where to put it. I can't answer the question. All I know about, the activities of President Tudjman at the time, I know from his interview, public appearances, during which he advocated a peaceful solution. He was always showing willingness to negotiate, and there are many traces of him trying to reach a peaceful solution for the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. You haven't read the presidential transcripts, where he said something to the contrary? Yes or no, sir.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to go, last of all, to P07570, P07570. This is a record of another meeting, in fact, very close in time, 12th of January, 1994, another meeting with President Tudjman. President Tudjman, at the middle of page 62, please, the same in the English and in the Croatian language, someone named Pranjic is talking about a particular situation, and President Tudjman comes in, in the middle of the page, and says: "President: All right. Tell me, have they perpetrated crimes in Krizancevo Selo? That's right. Please do not delude yourselves again. Do you know whom they removed? They have removed those who fought each other, you see, and I want to tell you something else, and we should be aware of this. They are howling against Mrcip [phoen] to me, but, gentlemen, I too am against that, but this was a life-and-death struggle from Vukovar to Gospic, and if it hadn't been people like these men, we would not have Croatia. Let's get that clear." Again, sir, isn't this a pure example of Tudjman saying, We need these people like this, we need the Vukojevics, we need the Mrcips, we need these people to get the job done; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm answering the same way. Based on this, I can't arrive at such conclusions. I can't establish a link with my expert report. This applies to a different situation, and it has nothing whatsoever to do with the crux and the purpose of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, the reason it doesn't have anything to do with your report is because you didn't review any of the documents related to this case. That's why you can say it has nothing to do with your report, because your report doesn't have anything to do with the facts of this case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you told us all afternoon you didn't read a single HVO document, you didn't review a single Herceg-Bosna document, you've never seen the documents before, I didn't consider the facts, I've never seen a presidential transcript. Is that -- well, you didn't, did you, sir? You didn't consider any of that material?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, my analysis referred to a socio-psychological context and the application of that context to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was dealing with a context, primarily context, and I used all the available literature that I used. I used the information for that level of my analysis from the publications that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tudjman says here, does he not, sir: "If it hadn't been for such men, we wouldn't have Croatia"; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sakic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have two questions I would like to put to you, Witness, and they -- or expert, may go, in fact, directly to your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The first refers to what is page 65, and there you speak of culture, system of value, identity, and you say that the human population has developed its diversity through genes, language, and culture. Do I have to understand you as saying that nationality is something that can be found in genes?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quoted Hofstetter [phoen], and I quoted him a lot. This is a theoretical presumption that is applied in anthropology, sociology, psychology, and partly in medicine that is currently dealing with the gene that exists in the origin of various species, and you know that medical scientists are involved in that. You know that nationality, at least partly, has to do with the genes, with culture, and with the language, and these three elements all make up the similarities between -- among the various members of the group. And in that, nationalities differ from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you're actually telling the Chamber, under oath, that Brits have a typical British gene, as French have a French gene, and the Germans have a German gene, and the Italians have an Italian gene, so that from a drop of blood one can say what nationality the person has?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is absolutely impossible to prove theoretically, and I never said that. I only said that medicine is involved in the study of the so-called hapletids [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, here you speak of identity and of diversity through genes. Now, I hear that you're saying that I cannot take this as it stands here because there is no possibility to identify nationality by analysing genes. I'm leaving open the question whether one day, one will find out. I will leave that open. But so far there is no research that shows that the French have different genes or a different gene as compared to the Germans; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question relates to page 12 of your report, and there you mention Wilhelm Wundt. You call him founder of experimental psychology. I'm not challenging that. But you refer to his book "Voelkerpsychologie," "Psychology of Peoples," in 10 volumes. Are you saying that this constitutes a valuable contribution? Can you tell me in what way this has been valuable?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a moment. I would like to correct something. Wilhelm Wundt was the founder of the experimental laboratory and the experimental psychology. This happened in Leipzig 1889. Second of all, I didn't say that it was a valuable contribution. It was just an overview. I drafted a small introduction, as is customary among the scientists, and I provided an overview showing from when this national and ethnical identities were being studied. As you can see, I also quoted Ibn Khaldun who studied ethnic identities of the indigenous tribes in Asia way back in the 14th and 15th century, so this is only an overview. I did not say that this was a valuable contribution. In my expert report, I relied on contemporary sociological studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, you have checked the translation, I suppose. Yes, please. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: This is your favourite topic, I know, and there is absolutely nothing like that in Croatian language, that this is valuable contribution, so the translation doesn't relate what was said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I take your word for it, unless someone -- THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Yeah, because I am able to read just one sentence in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, please. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] "From the first positivist phase, one should certainly mention the 10-volume book by the founder of experimental psychology, Wilhelm Wundt, 'The Psychology of Peoples,' an intra-cultural comparative psychological analyses of various countries based on the languages, mis-moral [as interpreted], arts, and laws."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prlic. A valuable contribution. Witness, do you know what today's evaluation of "Voelkerpsychologie" is? How is it regarded in contemporary science?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- it belongs to the history of psychology and is only used in the history of psychology when it is mentioned -- when you want to say where psychology started from and how it developed. It would not stand the test of time, the social identity theories as contemporaries, Tyfol [phoen], Turner, and all the people I mentioned in my report and which are contemporary theories. It wouldn't pass muster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware of the historical effects this theory had, the use that was made of "Voelkerpsychologie"?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I do know about that. It was used -- I know that it was used in Nazi Germany. However, that does not mean that if it was used there, it should be ascribed to the author. The author is a well-known name. It's the interpretations of the theory or re-interpretations, if I may say so, were used, and the author absolutely does not deserve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Wundt is not on trial here and I will not go further in this, but I still have another question. In your analysis, you speak rather in detail about historical developments and about Serb crimes. I have not found any relevance -- any reference in your whole report, but maybe this is an oversight, but I found no reference to the crimes of the Ustasha. Can you explain this? Do you think that this is an element which has absolutely no connection to the events of 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did mention the Ustashas in the context of an extremist organisation, and the crime in Jasenovac I also mention in my expert report and said that there were these extremist groups that had a vital influence on the future of Yugoslavia, and I describe all this in my expert report. And the greatest crimes -- well, the rest wasn't relevant or important for an analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just an additional small question. Would you agree to a statement which designs Jasenovac as a myth? Do you think that's a correct way of speaking of that place?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not deal with the question of Jasenovac. When you speak about myths in the social and psychological sense, then it is referred to as being an incorrect formulation of reality or something that is invented, but it can be a part of an ideology, too. And when we speak of the myth of Jasenovac, when that is mentioned, as far as I understand it, it means primarily the Serbian abuse with respect to the number of victims in Jasenovac, within the context of their aggressive aims against Croatia and the homogenisation of Serbs along that principle, in the sense that all Croats were Ustashas. So from that perspective, when we speak about the number, exclusively of figures, the number, and that number sometimes reached a million, you can speak about a myth because that is an invention of the fact that there were a million, but that there were 800.000 or whatever, that is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that I do have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the first thing I want to ask you is this: In view of the fact that the Prosecutor spent quite a lot of time insisting on and clearly putting to you his case, that you, in fact, assume that the events during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not organised and directed from top to bottom, that is the Prosecution's case, that's what the Prosecution is saying, that this was just your assumption and that you put that assumption forward. Can you tell me whether what the Prosecutor is alleging is correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, do you, in fact, presume in any way that those events in Bosnia were organised at the top, and managed and directed from the top downwards, and that they weren't spontaneous at all in the sense of these theories of social psychology that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not presuming that, and I didn't deal with that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So after the Prosecutor's interventions, do you, in fact, stand by -- stand entirely by the assertion and claims you made in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, yes, I stand entirely by what I said in my expert report, all my claims there, and I think that the expert report is homogenous, and that methodologically it is founded upon scientific theory, and that the applications were sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, linked to a series of questions asked by my colleague for the Prosecution, let's get one thing clear. As a scholar scientist, and also as a citizen in Croatia during the events in Croatia and later -- and also in Bosnia, what were you, in fact, interested on primarily and principally as a scholar, as a scientist, the details of the events or just the global processes?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, as a scientist, I was always interested in processes and global processes, national, local and global processes. That was what I dealt with, dealing with the war in Croatia as well, but my scientific activities were also geared towards organising public meetings, the internationalisation of the conflict. As it happened so contextualisation was very important for me in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In order to apply the modern theories of social psychology, is it at all necessary for you to know the details at a lower level, is that necessary, or does it suffice, for you to carry out your analysis, for the purposes you carried them out, to view just the global context of the events?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, for my analysis I used what was sufficient for me, and I said yesterday that for me to analyse events at a lower level, that I could do that, too, but then I would have to look at the event at that lower level. So you can use the same theoretical framework, but you apply it differently. There are such analyses, yes, but they are lower-level analyses, at lower levels. I could do that, but the approach would be different and then I would, of course, have to read the different individual documents and so on, different material. I would use different material for me to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were shown document P11027. It was the article from the "Nacional." Just a short question, and I would like an even shorter answer. You said that you denied the allegations and statements made in that article?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, we did deny them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there other situations in which either you, personally, or your institute denied what was written?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, there were a number of writings about the institute. We denied them every time. And as the director of the institute, I always dealt with these questions and denied any things that we -- the type of things that we heard raised here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And another question in that regard. Doctor, if the article were correct, would you then deny it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the article were correct, I wouldn't deny it, because there were quite a lot of articles about the institute that were quite proper and correct, praising the institute, in fact, as a respectable international institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as an example of the existence of disciplinary measures, sanctions, punishment in Bosnia within the HVO, the Prosecutor used document P02595. Let me remind you it's a document where a commander from Central Bosnia, Mario Cerkez in this case, pronounced a disciplinary measure against a soldier, a policeman in a brigade. Not to waste time, I think you remember that case. Now, tell me, since you dealt with a penology, and I'll have another question for you on that subject, do you know anything about -- well, you said you didn't know anything about that particular event and that particular document, but my question to you is this: Do you perhaps know anything about whether the disciplinary measure was implemented or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Doctor, precisely because you dealt with penology, the purpose of sanctioning perpetrators or punishing perpetrators is contained in two parts. Somebody has to make a decision and find somebody guilty of something, according to the law, and then those disciplinary measures have to be carried out; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, since you're an expert in penology, tell me, please, the decision, itself, about establishing disciplinary measures and punishment without applying it, without applying them, is there any sense in that and is anything achieved?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing is achieved either generally or specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a moment ago the Prosecutor asked you about Vice Vukojevic, and according to the Prosecutor, it is a notorious fact that Mr. Vice Vukojevic was an extremist nationalist, Croatian nationalist. You said you don't know him, personally, but perhaps from the press or in any other way, you might happen to know that he was taken to trial a number of times for libel in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote about that -- I read about that, as well as what we mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your expert report, the section where you talk about the model of behaviour of people in conflict, the model that you explained to us, can it be applied to a perfectly-established and well-disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These theories would not, of course, be as recognised as they are if they could not be applied globally, which means, in other words, they must be applicable to all phenomena on a global level. And also what the general talked about yesterday, the elements such as elemental disasters, rebellions, and so on, those theories must be able to be applied there, too. Otherwise, they would be revised or would have to be refuted and denied and then would have been relegated to history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, what is the probability of such irregularities and deviations appearing in a conflict involving only two highly-disciplined and organised militaries? And compare that with the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was completely different. Would that incidence be higher or lower?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they would be lower. Of course, they would be lower, and that is the meaning of training of modern armies. Every soldier has to be informed about the Geneva Conventions, has to be physically prepared, psychologically prepared, and it is only logical that such -- that incidents of such things would be lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doctor, the OTP tried to create an impression that you were not honest in your CV. Let me just ask you a very simple thing here. Is there anything in your life and in your activity, or are there many other things that are not in this curriculum?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This curriculum vitae contains my professional activity from 1979 until the present day, with the war episode, and there is nothing else that might describe me properly that is hidden from that curriculum.
