My life motto was always to primarily be governed by profession and science.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, I understand that you have played basketball a lot and that you're still active in the sport.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mean that type of activity. I was an active player of football, basketball, table tennis. I am a passionate athlete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you were to write a curriculum vitae to apply for a job in my company as a clerk, would you put it in your curriculum vitae that you were a good athlete?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. Maybe I would to brag, because if I put it in my CV, that I am an athlete, that would also mean that I am healthy, but if I was applying for a position of a clerk, I would -- I would put it in my CV that I speak languages, that I can use a personal computer, and something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In any case, the curriculum that you offer is the model that you use in your circles in your profession; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This curriculum vitae follows a European protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And my last question to you. The Prosecutor spent a lot of time asking you about the founders of your institute, and then he expanded that and asked you about some names, Zuzul, Tudjman, Josip Jurcevic, and so on and so forth. I would like to simplify that and ask you as follows: First of all, as a psychiatrist, as a professor, as a scientist, do you know many colleagues who share similar characteristics, people who belong to the same circle in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given my professional activities, the fact that I founded the department and participation in the work of the university, I have met almost the entire intellectual structure in the social and humanist areas in Croatia, people who hold doctoral degrees and higher, and that's why I was able to coordinate the foundation of a department. Anybody who embarks on such a job will know how demanding that job is. As far as my acquaintances are concerned, Zuzul and Tudjman are well-known scientists, and I socialised with them as scientists, and in the initial stages they participated in the foundation, then establishment of the institute. When the institute was finally established, they then joined the ranks of politicians and I remained working at the institute, and all my subsequent encounters with them were sporadic and informal. We were just acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you this, then: Professor, can one speak or can one say that given the size of that sub-cultural circle in Zagreb, in practical terms, you actually know everybody who belongs to that sub-cultural circle with the same characteristics? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there was another implication or an insinuation according to which the cultural circle, the intellectuals, when the aggression started, when Zagreb was shelled, did these people predominantly remain living in Zagreb, did they predominantly join the struggle in one way or another, or did they predominantly flee Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A vast majority remained in Zagreb, and a vast majority was involved in some defence tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were among them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you see that as a good act? Are you proud of yourself for that or do you feel ashamed for having responded to the call of your country to defend it from aggression?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I had not worked in the Ministry of Justice, I would have still joined. I would have harnessed my capabilities maybe not in the way I did in the Ministry of Justice, but I would offer my capabilities to join the defence of Croatia because there was no other way out, there was no other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are talking about your science here. Can the same thing be said about many other people, that they joined as best as they could and they found a place where they could be of the best use? Can one say that this was the general characteristic or the general model that prevailed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the case of general defence, and the public polls carried out by the Pilar Institute show that a majority of Croatian citizens, including intellectuals, were prepared to engage in the struggle for Croatia because they perceived a democratic and independent Croatia as their basic goal and they wanted to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Professor. Thank you very much for coming here and for testifying in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomanovic, earlier you mentioned the problem of the additional cross-examination. Remember that in its guide-line number 1, point 10, this is what the Chamber wrote: In the exceptional circumstances where the Trial Chamber authorised a party to have an additional cross-examination, this examination shall be limited to matters determined by the Chamber. Therefore, we have to have an exceptional case. And when Mr. Scott believes -- the Trial Chamber believes that when Mr. Scott talked about Mr. Prlic, he said nothing new because Mr. Prlic is in the indictment. Therefore, the Trial Chamber believes that there was nothing exceptional about this matter, and because of this, there is no need for an additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the interpretation, which took a bit longer. I absolutely agree with you, Your Honour, and at this moment I will not request time for additional cross-examination because nothing new has been said, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a minute. Judge Prandler has a few questions -- one question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Further questioned by the Court: Frankly, I should have asked my questions a bit earlier, but I was not quite aware of the fact that we finish today. Then I would like to come back to the end of the report and where the expert, in a way, taking into account all the factors of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it is -- these are from pages 101 and 102 and 3. And I only would like to ask the expert if he upholds his approach and conclusions when starting with page 101, he speaks about the, and I quote "basic determinants of the war in B and H in relation to causes, course of the war, and war group goals." And under this heading, actually, he mentions three, and the fourth one was also basic determinants. The first one, what he says, that the first and basic determinant of the war in B and H is aggression. Aggression was initiated by Serbia. It is the first conclusion. Now, the second fundamental determinant, again on page 101, he says that in the areas of Croatia and B and H, Serbia committed genocide, ethnic cleansing, culturalicide and urbicide, and he continues that it is the second fundamental determinant of the war in B and H. And then on page 102, then the third determinant, according to the expert, that is the ethnic conflict of or probably between Bosniak Muslims and Croats caused by Serbian aggression on B and H. And it is the third determinant. And, finally, the fourth determinant of the war is a continuation and finalisation in B and H relates to the inefficiency and wrong decisions of the international community, and not to prevent aggression and intentions of Serbia, as far as the aggression from Croatia to B and H territory. Now, my question is that, to the expert, to -- actually, to Professor Sakic, if you maintain your position that those main -- those four main determinants had to be mentioned in your report, when you summarised the position of yours concerning the war in B and H, noting that it has been done with all objectivity, scientific, to avoid any one-sidedness, and if you really feel that you still maintain these four factors as major determinants for the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do stand by all that, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Professor, your testimony is now over. I thank you, on behalf of my fellow Judges and myself, for having come here to testify for General Praljak's Defence, and I would like our usher to please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, next week we will be hearing your last witness. It will be the last witness of the Praljak Defence. After that, we will have an idle week, and then we will start with the first witness of the Petkovic Defence. Is that the way the schedule is supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards the Defence plan for General Praljak, as you said, we have a witness coming in on Monday. When we realised that we might get through Mr. Sakic, we thought we might change the schedule, but it was difficult to do that. It was not practical, there were a lot of difficulties, and therefore the witness will come in as planned on Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everything is crystal clear. Mr. Scott, do you have anything to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I hope everyone will have a few days off. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we'll have a few days, and we can use those days to read the thousands or millions of pages of documents. It will be very useful. And, of course, to get ready for the next witness on Monday. I wish you all a pleasant evening, and we will resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
